articles.title: Rochdale selected for £9.4m children’s mental health pilot
articles.excerpt: Breaking: Rochdale will join Stockport and Tameside in Care Together, bringing NHS mental health professionals into children’s social care teams from early 2027.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale has been selected for a new government mental health pilot designed to make support easier to access for children involved with social care and their families.

The Department of Health and Social Care has announced up to £9.4 million over three years for Care Together, which will operate across Rochdale, Stockport and Tameside.

Mental health professionals from existing NHS services will work within children's social care teams. The aim is to help families receive expert support earlier, with less difficulty navigating separate services.

NHS Greater Manchester Integrated Care Board will lead the programme alongside the three local authorities. It is expected to launch in early 2027 and run until 2029.

Who could benefit?

The department says up to 7,000 children and young people across the three participating boroughs could be covered, alongside their parents, carers and guardians. That figure covers all three boroughs combined. A separate allocation for Rochdale has not been provided in the announcement.

The groups identified include children in need, those on child protection plans, children in care, care leavers and adopted children.

Support could include family therapy and help for parents and primary caregivers, with services tailored to individual needs.

What will change for families?

Mental health professionals will work within social care settings, bringing expertise into the teams already supporting children and families.

The government hopes this will make it easier to identify needs and arrange appropriate help before problems reach crisis point. Faster access is an intended benefit of the pilot, with its effectiveness to be evaluated during the programme.

Dame Diana Johnson, Minister of State for Public Health and Patient Safety, said:

“For too long, fragmented mental health services have left young people in care, care leavers, parents, carers, and guardians not knowing where to turn for support.

“We are committed to change how we support young people, and this exciting and innovative pilot will see thousands more children across Greater Manchester get specialist mental health support based on their personal needs and in quicker time, before they reach crisis point.”

Children's Minister Josh MacAlister said children supported by social care can face severe mental health challenges because of trauma and adversity. He said the pilot forms part of wider efforts to support vulnerable young people as they move into adult life.

Professor Manisha Kumar, Chief Clinical Officer at NHS Greater Manchester, said the programme would help partners provide earlier support that takes account of children's experiences and wider family circumstances.

She said learning from the work in Rochdale, Stockport and Tameside would also help shape changes nationally.

When will Care Together start?

The pilot is expected to launch in early 2027 and run until 2029. An evaluation will assess whether the approach could be extended to other parts of the country.

The announcement does not yet specify how many Rochdale families will receive support, how referrals will work or which local teams will take part.

For local families, those practical details will matter: who can access help, how quickly it becomes available and whether bringing services together makes support easier to obtain.

What would make the biggest difference to mental health support for children and families in Rochdale? Share your thoughts in the comments, while protecting children's privacy and avoiding details that could identify them.

articles.title: Urgent appeal to find woman after suspected human tissue discovered in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Police fear a woman who may have recently given birth needs urgent medical attention after a discovery near Watkins Street and Charter Street, off Kingsway.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING NEWS | ONGOING AND DEVELOPING STORY. This report will be updated when further verified information becomes available.

Detectives are trying to find a woman who may need urgent medical attention after suspected human tissue was discovered off Kingsway in Rochdale.

Greater Manchester Police said evidence found near the junction of Watkins Street and Charter Street suggests a woman may have recently given birth. Officers were called shortly before 9am on Thursday 22 October.

Police have been examining the scene and carrying out enquiries. Their priority is to find the woman and make sure she is safe and well.

Detective Inspector Daniel Daly, from GMP's Rochdale CID, said: “She may be in need of urgent medical attention, and she is our absolute priority at the moment - that is why we are asking anyone with information to contact us.”

Anyone with information, or who may have seen a woman in distress, should call 101 and quote incident number 684 of 22/10/2026.

Information can also be reported online or through GMP's LiveChat service at https://www.gmp.police.uk. Alternatively, contact Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111.

DI Daly asked the public not to speculate: “We would ask that people don't speculate on the circumstances of this discovery as it hinders our investigation and is upsetting for those involved.”

The information in this report comes from Greater Manchester Police's appeal issued on 22 October 2026. Police have not confirmed further circumstances in that appeal.

Two vehicles were seized by police in Heywood after drivers ignored a school crossing patrol, highlighting ongoing concerns about road safety near schools.

Police in Heywood have seized two vehicles after drivers failed to stop for a school crossing patrol. The incident occurred when Mr. Jones, the crossing patrol officer, was already standing in the road as the vehicles approached. Fortunately, no injuries were reported during these incidents.

Councillor Williams expressed his dismay at the incidents, stating that such behaviour is unacceptable and poses a significant risk to children. In response to these ongoing safety issues, police have been using body-worn cameras in hotspot areas to deter dangerous driving.

The seizure of these vehicles underscores the need for increased vigilance and compliance with road safety regulations, particularly near schools. Local residents and parents are encouraged to remain alert and report any similar incidents to the authorities.

articles.title: Are there really fairies in Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: Short answer: no—there’s no evidence for supernatural visitors, but the place-name, a nineteenth‑century literary tradition and a distinctive rock ‘chapel’ have combined to make Healey Dell one of Rochdale’s best-loved bits of local folklore.
articles.summary: Short answer: no—there’s no evidence for supernatural visitors, but the place-name, a nineteenth‑century literary tradition and a distinctive rock ‘chapel’ have combined to make Healey Dell one of Rochdale’s best-loved bits of local folklore.
articles.body:
Ask a local where the Fairies’ Chapel is and they’ll point you down the steps from Station Road, into the ravine by the River Spodden. Ask whether fairies live there and the practical answer is simple: no verifiable evidence supports the existence of fairies; what the records do show is a named rock formation, a cluster of old stories collected in the nineteenth century and a long history of people visiting the site because the place feels, to many, a little uncanny. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

Those are not trivial facts. Healey Dell is a designated Local Nature Reserve and an area of industrial archaeology that straddles borough boundaries; part of the valley was legally made a statutory LNR in April 1976. The most dramatic built feature is the Healey Dell Viaduct, a high, eight‑arched sandstone railway viaduct that is a Grade II listed structure on the National Heritage List for England. Those designations are documentary and can be checked. ([rossendale.gov.uk](https://www.rossendale.gov.uk/download/meetings/id/4148/e2_appendix_2))

The Dell’s historical record is everyday, material and useful. The valley contains the remains of nineteenth‑century mills and the disused Rochdale‑to‑Bacup railway line; archaeological and conservation surveys catalogue those features and guide how the reserve is managed for wildlife and visitors. Management is led locally by Rochdale (and neighbouring Rossendale) authorities and by volunteer groups; published ecological reports and neighbourhood plans reference Healey Dell when mapping green infrastructure for the area. That is the part of the story that affects readers’ lives—path repairs, parking signage, listed‑building consent for the viaduct—because those are things the council, landowners and statutory consultees can change. ([rmnf.org.uk](https://www.rmnf.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Vol-1-Healey-Dell-Final-Report.pdf))

The Fairies’ Chapel and the Healey Dwarf belong to a different archive: folklore. Nineteenth‑century writers and local collectors, notably the county antiquarian tradition and later local compilers, set down tales about a natural recess in the rock that looked a little like an altar and could be called a chapel. Early print references—quoted in modern guides—describe a hidden pulpit‑like formation revealed when a flood washed away a covering ledge; later colourful retellings add a Fairy Queen, a Fairy King and a bewitched dwarf or witch‑figure, motifs common to British fairy lore. Those stories come from literary and folkloric sources rather than parish registers, court records or archaeological excavation reports; they are valuable for what they tell us about local imagination and nineteenth‑century reading habits, not as evidence of the supernatural. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

You can still see the place‑name on the ground. Local walking leaflets and heritage trails mark a route down to the feature and signposts to a ‘Fairy Chapel’ appear on nearby footpaths and at the steps off Station Road. Community events and the Tearooms’ heritage material reproduce the old legends for visitors, which keeps the stories alive. None of these modern references change the distinction: a name, an attractive rock formation and repeated storytelling are not proof of otherworldly residents. ([whitworth.gov.uk](https://www.whitworth.gov.uk/uploads/walkingdocuments/files/WALK%206%20Healey%20Dell%20-%20captioned%20viaduct.pdf))

What remains uncertain—and worth noting—is provenance. Some of the best‑known versions of the Healey tales were shaped by nineteenth‑century collectors and local storytellers; when folklore circulates in print, oral tradition and tourism literature it can harden into ‘local history’ in popular memory. Where claims involve specific historical persons, dates or events, they should be tested against archival material; in the case of the Fairies’ Chapel, the archive records the place and the stories about it, not supernatural events. If you want proof, visit the council‑maintained reserve, look up the Historic England listing for the viaduct and read the nineteenth‑century sources for yourself—then decide whether the place’s atmosphere does the rest. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1317784))

articles.title: Rochdale Council Rejects Takeaway Application on Health Grounds
articles.excerpt: Plans for a new takeaway at 159 Yorkshire Street in Rochdale have been rejected by the council due to concerns over public health and the existing number of fast-food outlets in the area.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has refused an application for a new takeaway at 159 Yorkshire Street, citing health concerns related to the high number of existing fast-food establishments in the area. The proposal, submitted by Sheeraz Ahmed, aimed to convert the former Ria Money Transfer shop into a takeaway primarily focused on collection and delivery.

The application detailed plans for a business serving a variety of hot food products, including burgers, fried chicken, pizzas, kebabs, desserts, waffles, and milkshakes. It included internal alterations to create customer serving areas, food preparation spaces, and cooking facilities. The proposed opening hours were set from 11am to 11pm, and the establishment was expected to create four new jobs.

However, the council's planning officer raised concerns regarding the potential impact on local eating habits. The Public Health officer noted that the application would increase the availability of food high in fat, salt, and sugar. Furthermore, it was highlighted that a health impact assessment had not been conducted, leading to the recommendation that the development should not be approved.

This decision reflects ongoing efforts by Rochdale Council to manage the proliferation of fast-food outlets in the town centre, aiming to promote healthier eating habits among residents. The refusal of this application may influence future proposals for similar establishments in the area.

Sheeraz Ahmed applied to Rochdale Council for permission to turn a shop into a fast-food takeaway at 159 Yorkshire Street, Rochdale. The site had most recently been home to Ria Money Transfer. In documents submitted with the application, Building Design Services said: “The proposal seeks to introduce a takeaway business operating primarily as a collection and delivery-based food establishment serving a variety of hot food products, including burgers, fried chicken, pizzas, kebabs, desserts, waffles and milkshakes. “The proposed development would involve internal alterations to facilitate the operation of the takeaway, including the provision of customer serving areas, food preparation spaces, cooking facilities, staff welfare facilities and ancillary storage areas. “The premises would operate as a takeaway only establishment with no internal seating proposed for customers.” The proposed opening hours were from 11am to 11pm and the takeaway would have created four jobs. But the application raised concerns about people’s eating habits and the number of fast-food restaurants and takeaways already in the area. A planning officer’s report referenced the council’s Public Health officer, who noted: “The planning application will increase the availability of food high in fat, salt, and sugar, and a health impact assessment has not been carried out, and as such I request that the development is not approved. READ MORE: Town centre reclaims Britain in Bloom crown “From a Public Health perspective, applications for fast-food outlets should be refused in locations where there is evidence that a concentration of such uses is having an adverse impact on local health, pollution or anti-social-behaviour, or where they are within walking distance of schools and other places where children and young people congregate.” The planning officer added: “Public Health also identifies that obesity levels within both Rochdale and the Central Rochdale Ward exceed national averages and concludes that the proposal would further increase access to unhealthy food choices within an area already experiencing poor health outcomes. “Public Health has further advised that no health impact assessment has been undertaken and that the application has not demonstrated that the proposal would not have an adverse impact on health outcomes.” Refusing the application, the council said: “The proposal would increase the proportion of hot-food takeaway premises within Yorkshire Street Local Centre to approximately 21.7% of commercial ground-floor units, exceeding the 20% threshold set out within the council’s adopted Guidelines and Standards for Hot Food Takeaways SPD. “The Director of Public Health and Communities has identified that there are already 13 hot-food takeaway premises within 400 metres of the application site and 30 such premises within the ward and has provided evidence that obesity levels within both Rochdale and Central Rochdale Ward exceed national averages. “The proposal would further increase the concentration of hot-food takeaway uses within an area where adverse health outcomes have been identified. “Insufficient evidence has been submitted to demonstrate that the proposed development would not contribute to those identified health concerns or to justify a departure from the council’s adopted policy approach.” SUPPORT THE ROCHDALE TIMES: FOLLOW US ON FACEBOOK Got a story? articles.title: Doorman Highlights Normalisation of Racial Abuse After Incident at Ko-Ko Lounge
articles.excerpt: Jawad Ali, a doorman at Ko-Ko Lounge in Rochdale, has raised concerns about the increasing normalisation of racial abuse following a recent incident involving a club-goer.
articles.content_html:
A doorman at Ko-Ko Lounge in Rochdale has raised concerns about the normalisation of racial abuse after witnessing a disturbing incident on Saturday night. Jawad Ali, 20, reported that a woman became aggressive and shouted racial slurs at a black security guard when asked to move away from an exit.

The incident, captured on video and shared widely online, shows the woman making derogatory gestures towards the guard. Ali, who was working for Protective One Security at the time, described the behaviour as "disgusting" and stated that he now expects such incidents during his shifts.

Greater Manchester Police confirmed they have received a report regarding the incident and are currently conducting inquiries. Ali alleged that the woman also directed racial abuse towards him before the video was recorded.

This incident raises significant concerns about the treatment of security staff and the prevalence of racial abuse in nightlife settings. As investigations continue, it highlights the need for greater awareness and action against such behaviour.

articles.title: Rochdale Crowned Champion at Britain in Bloom Awards 2026
articles.excerpt: Rochdale has been awarded gold and crowned the overall winner in the Town Centres and City Centres category at the Britain in Bloom awards, showcasing the town's commitment to community participation and regeneration efforts.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale has been awarded gold and crowned the overall winner in the Town Centres and City Centres category at the Britain in Bloom awards for 2026. This recognition highlights the town's ongoing commitment to enhancing its public spaces and fostering community involvement in local beautification efforts.

The competition featured 44 finalists, with Rochdale outperforming other notable entries such as Floral Godalming, Shaftesbury in Bloom, and Sidcup Partners Limited. This victory follows a previous gold award won by Rochdale in 2024, demonstrating a consistent dedication to improving the town's environment and aesthetics.

Significant regeneration efforts have taken place in Rochdale in recent years, including the transformation of Broadfield Park slopes, which have contributed to the town's appeal. The award reflects not only the physical improvements but also the strong community participation that has been integral to these initiatives.

Rochdale's success in the Britain in Bloom awards is a testament to the hard work of local volunteers and businesses, who have played a crucial role in supporting these efforts. The town centre is set to champion the borough's achievements as it moves forward, showcasing the positive impact of community collaboration.

Published: 22 October 2026 Rochdale is celebrating a blooming brilliant victory after striking gold at this year’s Britain in Bloom awards and being crowned the overall winner of the Town Centres and City Centres category. Rochdale was placed ahead of Floral Godalming (Southeast), Shaftesbury in Bloom (South) and Sidcup Partners Limited (London). Rochdale in Bloom has a proud competition record, securing gold in 2018, being named Best Small City in 2022 and winning gold again for Rochdale town centre in 2024. This year’s category win keeps the title in the borough after Middleton town centre took the top prize last year. Rochdale has undergone significant regeneration in recent years. The Grade I-listed Rochdale Town Hall has been expertly restored, complemented by the creation of the new Town Hall Square and the transformation of the Broadfield Park slopes. Supported by a multi-million-pound National Lottery Heritage Fund grant, have made this historic quarter the envy of many. Judges praised Rochdale town centre’s vibrant displays from Bowlee Garden Nursery, recycling initiatives and exceptional cleanliness, as well as the pride, teamwork and dedication of everyone involved. They also recognised the commitment to local biodiversity and strong partnerships, with Rochdale exceeding the gold standard in horticulture, environmental responsibility and community participation. Rochdale’s historic Baillie Street Quarter and striking murals, created through the 2025 Rochdale Common Walls Festival, strengthened the town centre’s entry by showcasing its culture and civic pride. Councillor Tricia Ayrton, deputy leader and cabinet member for climate change and environment at Rochdale Borough Council, said: “What another outstanding achievement for our borough. Last year, Middleton town centre achieved gold and was overall category winner and now Rochdale town centre is back as a worthy winner once again championing our borough for 2026. “This gold belongs to every volunteer, business, Rochdale Town Centre BID, Rochdale Riverside and the council’s environmental management team whose hard work keeps our public spaces looking their best. It’s a celebration of far more than flowers – it’s about pride in our town and brilliant working partnerships.  Together, we’ve shown the country what Rochdale can achieve and hosting the national awards in the Northwest for the first time, at our magnificent Rochdale Town Hall, made this triumph even more special.” Teresa Potter, RHS Britain in Bloom judge, commented: “Huge congratulations to you all, a well-deserved success. You were in a good category with excellent entries. Richard and I had the best week of judging this year. Wishing you and your fellow entrants the very best for the coming bloom year. This one has been a joy once again.” More on the boroughs in bloom awards Related content Councillor Tricia Ayrton Council news from across the borough of Rochdale Parks and open spaces Was this page helpful? articles.title: Martlet Kitchen in Rochdale Wins International Recognition
articles.excerpt: Martlet Kitchen, located in Rochdale, has been ranked among the top-rated restaurants globally, celebrating its second anniversary with an international award.
articles.content_html:
Martlet Kitchen, a restaurant in Rochdale, has recently achieved international recognition by being ranked among the top-rated restaurants globally. This accolade comes as the establishment celebrates its second birthday, marking a significant milestone in its journey since opening.

The restaurant has been rated in the top 10 percent of all establishments on TripAdvisor, highlighting its commitment to quality and customer satisfaction. Martlet Kitchen is known for its focus on using top-quality local ingredients, which has contributed to its growing reputation in the culinary scene.

Local supplier Grandpa Greene’s plays a vital role in providing ingredients for Martlet Kitchen, further emphasising the restaurant's dedication to supporting local businesses. The restaurant aims to continue its success and is looking forward to achieving more accolades in the future.

In addition to Martlet Kitchen, other local establishments such as Shibden Mill Inn and The Fleece Inn have also been recognised with 2 AA rosettes, showcasing the high standard of dining available in the area. Martlet Kitchen prides itself on delivering excellent service, which has undoubtedly played a part in its recent achievements.

Published: 22 October 2026 Rochdale Town Hall’s Martlet Kitchen has picked up the Trip Advisor Travellers’ Choice Award 2026, placing it among the top-rated restaurants in the world on the popular review site. The award honours businesses which consistently receive great reviews, with their scores placing them in the top 10 per cent of all establishments registered on the popular review site. With millions of businesses from around the globe listed on the site, the award is a huge accolade for the Martlet Kitchen, which recently celebrated its second birthday. It’s not the first time the restaurant, which specialises in traditional, high-quality British food, has been lauded. In his food column for The Guardian, legendary food critic Jay Rayner, described the Martlet Kitchen as a ‘victory of professionalism, good sense and, most of all, great taste and skill’ when he visited shortly after its opening in 2024. The Martlet Kitchen is helmed by multi award winning chef, Darren Parkinson, who trained at Hopwood Hall College before working at acclaimed establishments including Shibden Mill Inn in Halifax and the Fleece Inn in Ripponden, both of which boast 2 AA rosettes. Rooted in the community, its food and drink is sourced from the local area, including Milnrow’s Jacksons Farm, Defiance Distillery at Spotland Mill and Grandpa Greene’s in Oldham. Commenting on the win, Darren said: “This award is great news and we’re aiming for more accolades in the future. It’s about good old fashioned British grub, cooked to perfection, using top quality local ingredients, coupled with excellent service.” Restaurant Manager, Sarah Crabtree, said: “I’m so proud of what we’ve achieved. I think one of the keys to the Martlet’s success is that we change the menu regularly to keep it fresh and seasonal, but we also keep the old favourites that people particularly enjoy, like fish and chips. Everyone who works here takes huge pride in their job, so the experience for the customers is really consistent. You know you will get excellent service and food every time you come in.” As well as breakfast and lunch, the Martlet Kitchen offers a fine dining experience on Saturday nights and a Friday grill club. The venue’s unique setting in the Grade I-listed Rochdale Town Hall has also enabled it to offer unique experiences, with a recently launched private dining offer giving guests the chance to dine in the Mayor’s reception room. Councillor Sue Smith, cabinet member for communities and culture, said: “When we spearheaded the restoration of the town hall, with the support for the National Lottery Heritage Fund, we wanted every part of its operation to live up to this building’s grandeur and The Martlet Kitchen has delivered this in spades. To have our visitors place it among the top restaurants in operation is incredibly special and long may people enjoy this wonderful place.” Related content Councillor Sue Smith Council news from across the borough of Rochdale The Martlet Kitchen Was this page helpful? articles.title: East Lancashire Railway steam gala draws more than 2,000 passengers as numbers rise 21.4 per cent
articles.excerpt: Four visiting engines, late trains and a tribute to preservation pioneer Richard Greenwood marked a busy autumn gala on the heritage railway serving Heywood.
articles.content_html:
More than 2,000 passengers visited East Lancashire Railway's Autumn Steam Gala as four visiting locomotives helped deliver a 21.4 per cent increase in passenger numbers on last year's event, according to the railway.

The heritage line, which serves Heywood, held the gala from 16 to 18 October. Three of the four visiting engines were making their first appearances on the ELR, with autumn colours along the Irwell Valley providing the backdrop to a packed weekend of passenger trains, goods workings and late evening journeys.

A first visit from the Bluebell Railway

One of the headline visitors was South Eastern & Chatham Railway Class O1 No. 65, which travelled from the Bluebell Railway for what the ELR described as its furthest ever visit north.

Built at Ashford in 1896 and rebuilt into its present form in 1908, No. 65 appeared in ornate green SECR Wainwright goods livery. It joined resident Lancashire & Yorkshire engines 1300 and 752 in marking significant anniversaries connected with 1896.

Both resident engines received fresh paintwork in lined Lancashire & Yorkshire livery for the gala. No. 1300's finishing touches were completed the day before the event by the railway's resident Heritage Painters team.

Last chance to ride behind visiting pannier tank

Great Western pannier tank No. 7714 arrived from the Severn Valley Railway, courtesy of the SVR Pannier Tank Fund. Built in Stoke-on-Trent by Kerr, Stuart & Co. in 1930, the engine faced south during the gala, giving photographers a different view of the line.

Photographic run pasts with the railway's goods train at Burrs Country Park raised £493 in cash donations. The ELR says passengers have a final opportunity to travel behind No. 7714 on 24 and 25 October before it returns to the West Midlands.

LSWR S15 No. 30506, owned by the Urie Locomotive Society and visiting from the Mid Hants Railway, returned to the ELR for the first time since the 1993 Festival of Steam. It is due to haul scheduled steam services on 31 October and 1 November, as well as taking part in a photographic charter.

The fourth visitor, Hudswell Clarke No. 1208, also made its ELR debut. Usually based at the Embsay & Bolton Abbey Railway and owned by Stephen Middleton, the industrial tank engine worked shuttles to Ramsbottom and paired with No. 65. It carried names from different stages of its working life, including Harold, Illingworth and Mitchell.

Remembering a preservation pioneer

Resident engines City of Wells, Standard 4MT No. 80097 and Lancashire & Yorkshire Pug No. 11243 also featured during the weekend.

Friday included a tribute to preservation pioneer Richard Greenwood, who died earlier this year. Engines 752 and City of Wells, both associated with his preservation work, ran together while his family and friends travelled in the Lancashire & Yorkshire Directors Saloon. The railway said his ashes were scattered into the firebox as the train departed.

Saturday's programme continued after dark, with brake van journeys behind visiting Southern engines, a rare trip into Rawtenstall's bay platform and late passenger workings.

More than 250 volunteer turns

The ELR said more than 250 volunteer turns were needed to deliver the weekend.

General manager Lee Kenny said: “These are results that everyone involved can take pride in. They reflect a great deal of work before the first train runs, throughout the weekend and after the last visitors have gone home.”

He thanked the crews, station teams, stewards, cleaners, catering staff and those responsible for preparing and maintaining the railway, alongside the small team organising the event.

“The gala depends on people across the railway working together, and we are very grateful for the effort and commitment that went into this year's event,” he said.

The railway said the passenger increase helped raise funds for ongoing preservation. Transport for No. 65 was supported by the East Lancashire Railway Preservation Society and a private individual.

What is coming next?

The Lancashire & Yorkshire Running Day on 14 November is due to feature engines 752 and 1300 together on the steam service. Pug No. 11243 is also expected to offer short driver experiences around Bury Bolton Street station limits for a small fee. The Directors Saloon is due to offer another opportunity to travel.

The ELR has also announced provisional enthusiast event dates for 2027, when it will mark 40 years since reopening between Bury and Ramsbottom:

6 February: Winter Warmer Diesel Running Day.

19 February: Roch Valley L&Y Pug Railtour Anniversary, with brake van specials planned to mark 60 years since the final Whitworth branch railtours.

20 February: Lancashire & Yorkshire Running Day.

12 to 14 March: Spring Steam Gala.

10 April: Lancashire & Yorkshire Running Day.

1 to 4 July: Summer Diesel Gala.

23 to 25 July: 40th Anniversary of the ELR Gala.

11 September: L&YR Running Day.

24 to 26 September: Autumn Diesel Gala.

15 to 17 October: Autumn Steam Gala.

6 November: L&YR Running Day.

These dates and locomotive appearances are provisional. Check the railway's latest information before travelling at https://www.eastlancsrailway.org.uk.

Anyone interested in volunteering can find details of departments and recruitment tours at https://www.elrps.co.uk/volunteering.
